meta.title: Ticks: Hard & Soft Ticks

blocks.x: Ticks are obligatory blood-feeding ectoparasites of the class Arachnida, order Metastigmata, divided into two families with very different lifestyles: the hard ticks (Ixodidae) and the soft ticks (Argasidae). Both groups are medically important as vectors of some of the world's most significant vector-borne diseases.

Teardrop-shaped, bear a rigid dorsal scutum, and have an anteriorly visible capitulum. They feed for days at a time, show marked sexual dimorphism, and include genera such as Ixodes, Dermacentor, Rhipicephalus, and Boophilus.

Leathery, wrinkled, and lacking a scutum, with a ventral capitulum hidden from above. They feed rapidly (30–60 minutes), take repeated small blood meals across a long adult life, and include Ornithodoros, Argas, and Otobius.

Both groups are hemimetabolous (egg → larva → nymph → adult, no pupal stage), but differ sharply in host use: hard ticks are commonly one-, two-, or three-host ticks with a single nymphal stage, while soft ticks pass through several nymphal instars and multiple short-duration host attachments.

Hard ticks transmit Lyme disease, tick-borne encephalitis, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, babesiosis, and several arboviruses. Soft ticks transmit tick-borne relapsing fever and are implicated in Q-fever and African swine fever virus transmission. Both can cause tick paralysis.
Hard (Ixodid) ticks are the larger and better-studied of the two tick families, with a rigid body plan built for prolonged, forceful attachment to a host.

items: Ticks are obligatory ectoparasites that exhibit hematophagy (blood feeding).
Called "hard" ticks because they can resist the force of a human foot.
Bites are characteristically painless.
They thrive in areas of high humidity and often congregate in tight clumps in large numbers.
Blood loss to infested animals can be significant.
Hosts are detected by body odour; ticks have unique sensory organs that detect changes in temperature and air currents.
Sexual dimorphism is marked — males and females look distinctly different.
Global distribution includes species implicated in α-Gal syndrome (AGS) across at least 17 countries, including the United States, Australia, and much of Europe.
Hard-bodied ticks are shaped like a tear drop.
An anterior gnathosoma / capitulum projects forward, bearing the epistome, hypostome, chelicerae, and paired palps (4).
The idiosoma has a leg-bearing region called the podosoma.
Stigmata (spiracles) may be present and differ in number and position.
Festoons (wrinkles) are present on the body margins.
A scutum — the hard chitinous dorsal shield — is present and is notably large in males.
Sclerotised plates are present on the ventral surface.
Huge salivary glands are present.
The midgut has diverticula that allow great expansion to accommodate large volumes of blood.
Malpighian tubules form the excretory organs.
A pair of spiracles is situated lateroventrally.

blocks.x: Hard ticks develop through a simple, hemimetabolous life cycle, but the number of hosts used along the way varies by genus — a distinction with major implications for disease transmission.

blocks.x: Females lay large numbers of eggs — 1,000 to 20,000 — in a gelatinous mass; egg laying may last up to 5 weeks.
One larval instar, bearing six legs.
One nymphal instar, bearing eight legs.
Flat and oval, with mouthparts visible at the anterior end. Females take large volumes of blood and feed for up to four weeks; males take smaller blood meals and remain attached for a short time.
Hard ticks are classified by how many different hosts they use across their development:

In a classic three-host life cycle (e.g. Dermacentor variabilis, the American dog tick), the larva, nymph, and adult each feed on a separate host, dropping off between stages to moult in the environment.
Hard ticks are vectors of viral, bacterial, and protozoan pathogens, and their bites can themselves cause disease. Control ranges from simple personal protection to large-scale community programmes.

items: Tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) — caused by a flavivirus, transmitted primarily by Ixodes ricinus and Ixodes persulcatus.
Powassan virus
Arboviruses — Colorado tick fever, Russian spring-summer encephalitis, Omsk hemorrhagic fever
Lyme disease, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato — the most common vector-borne disease in North America and Europe.
Anaplasmosis (Anaplasma phagocytophilum) and ehrlichiosis (Ehrlichia chaffeensis).
Tick-borne typhus fever — including Rocky Mountain spotted fever, South African tick typhus, and Kenyan tick typhus.
Babesiosis, caused by intraerythrocytic protozoa of the genus Babesia (primarily B. microti in North America and B. divergens in Europe).
Tick paralysis — an acute ascending paralysis, often fatal, caused by neurotoxins in tick saliva.
Otoacariasis — ticks lodging in the ear.
Dermatosis — inflammation, itching, and ulceration that can progress to myiasis.
Envenomization at the bite site.
Exsanguination leading to anaemia in heavily infested hosts.

blocks.x: High vector potency in hard ticks results from a combination of traits:

items: Persistent, slow blood feeders, which permits wide pathogen distribution during a single meal.
Highly sclerotized bodies.
Few natural enemies.
Long longevity.
High reproductive potential.
Avoidance of fields and forests infested with ticks.
Repellents and impregnated clothing.
Careful removal: forceps, applying a hot object, chloroform, or coating the tick with oil, paraffin, nail polish, or Vaseline.
Insecticides such as organophosphates and pyrethroids.
Surveillance
Vegetation management
Host management
Targeted chemical control
Cultural practices
Personal protection

blocks.x: Soft ticks belong to a separate family from hard ticks and differ from them in body form, feeding behaviour, and life history — while sharing some of the same medical significance.

items: Ornithodoros moubata — the African relapsing fever tick, found only in Africa.
Argas persicus — the fowl tick.
Otobius megnini — the spinose ear tick (worldwide distribution).
Flat and oval shaped.
Tough, wrinkled, leathery, granulated bodies.
The capitulum is ventral and subterminal, or distant from the anterior margin (not visible from above).
The part of the body beyond the capitulum is called the hood.
No scutum (dorsal shield) — hence "soft" ticks.
The capitulum bears leg-like palps, a toothed hypostome, and a pair of chelicerae (smooth with sharp teeth at the tip).
Four pairs of legs.
Eyes may be present on the lateral margins.
A coxal gland opens between the coxae of the 1st and 2nd pairs of feet.
The anus is easy to see.
The midgut has numerous branching diverticula and can ingest blood up to 8× its own body weight.
Coxal glands filter off excess fluids and salts.
Gene's organ secretes waxy, waterproof liquids that coat the eggs.
Female adults lay 200–300 eggs in cracks and crevices, in the resting places of rodents, birds, and other animals.
Adults can live for many years (5 to 14 years).
The life cycle is hemimetabolous: eggs hatch into a six-legged larva, which moults into an eight-legged nymph.
There are 4 to 8 nymphal instars, each requiring at least one blood meal.
Duration from egg hatching to adult is 6–12 months.
Soft ticks attach for short periods, unlike many hard ("host") ticks that remain attached for days.
Tick-borne relapsing fever, caused by the spirochaete Borrelia duttoni; rodents, squirrels, and other domestic animals serve as reservoirs, and it is transmitted by the Ornithodoros moubata complex.
Q-fever, caused by a rickettsia, and also transmitted by consuming contaminated milk and food from domestic livestock.
Tick-borne relapsing fever can also be caused by other Borrelia species, including B. hermsii, B. turicatae, and B. hispanica.
African swine fever virus (ASFV) is a significant viral pathogen associated with soft ticks.
Tick paralysis — caused by neurotoxins in the saliva of certain tick species from both Ixodidae and Argasidae, affecting humans and animals worldwide.
Removal using forceps.
Heat, e.g. a glowing cigarette butt.
Coating with Vaseline, nail varnish, etc.
Applying chloroform, ether, etc.
Applying repellents.
Residual insecticide spray in homes, nests, and burrows.

blocks.x: Although both families are blood-feeding arachnids with hemimetabolous life cycles, their body plan and feeding strategy diverge sharply — differences that drive very different transmission dynamics for the diseases they carry.

items: Both are members of Class Arachnida, Order Metastigmata.
Both are obligatory ectoparasites exhibiting hematophagy.
Both have a hemimetabolous life cycle: egg → larva → nymph → adult.
Both can transmit serious human and animal pathogens and cause tick paralysis.
Both can be removed with forceps, heat, or by coating/suffocating agents such as Vaseline or chloroform.
Hard ticks are built for prolonged attachment (days to weeks); soft ticks feed briefly and repeatedly.
Hard ticks generally have one larval and one nymphal instar; soft ticks pass through several nymphal instars.
Hard ticks lay one large batch of eggs per lifetime; soft females lay smaller batches repeatedly across a lifespan that can reach 5–14 years.
Hard tick host-use strategy (one-, two-, or three-host) differs fundamentally from the soft tick pattern of many brief attachments to nest-dwelling hosts.
